title: How to go from count of milliseconds since epoch into a sys-time?
description:
If you're given `1762527600000`, which is `"2025-11-07 10:00:00 EST"` but in milliseconds, how to convert to a millisecond precision sys-time?

Can't go through `duration_milliseconds()` because it requires integers and that is >integer.max

Don't want to blindly allow doubles everywhere because they can be fractional, and because large double whole numbers are not precisely represented.

Maybe could add `duration_parse(x, precision =)` that takes a character `x` and parses it into an `int64_t` at C level and stores it at the requested precision. Then you can `as_sys_time()` that.

title: `date_time_parse_UTC()`? A more flexible `date_time_parse_RFC_3339()`
description:
`date_time_parse_RFC_3339()` is unique because it parses the RFC 3339 format, like:

```
2019-01-01T00:00:00Z
2019-01-01T00:00:00+0430
2019-01-01T00:00:00+04:30
```

Notably it allows you to parse and use the `+04:30` info. But it's pretty strict about the format itself. You can only customize `separator = "T"` and `offset = "Z"`.

This is an example where the abstraction over sys-time leaks:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/79043367/how-to-read-in-a-character-datetime-with-a-timezone-offset-in-r/79044161#79044161

```
2019-01-01 00:00+04:30
```

Notably, _no seconds_! We have to dip down to `sys_time_parse()` to parse this

```r
library(clock)

x <- c(
  "2023-10-29 00:00+02:00",
  "2023-10-29 01:00+02:00",
  "2023-10-29 02:00+02:00",
  "2023-10-29 02:00+01:00",
  "2023-10-29 03:00+01:00",
  "2023-10-29 04:00+01:00"
)

# Parse into (roughly) UTC, respecting `%Ez`, i.e. the `+HH:MM` bit
x <- sys_time_parse(
  x,
  format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M%Ez",
  precision = "minute"
)
x
#> <sys_time<minute>[6]>
#> [1] "2023-10-28T22:00" "2023-10-28T23:00" "2023-10-29T00:00" "2023-10-29T01:00"
#> [5] "2023-10-29T02:00" "2023-10-29T03:00"

# Convert to POSIXct with your expected time zone
as_date_time(x, zone = "Europe/Paris")
#> [1] "2023-10-29 00:00:00 CEST" "2023-10-29 01:00:00 CEST"
#> [3] "2023-10-29 02:00:00 CEST" "2023-10-29 02:00:00 CET" 
#> [5] "2023-10-29 03:00:00 CET"  "2023-10-29 04:00:00 CET"

# Or UTC if you wanted that
as_date_time(x, zone = "UTC")
#> [1] "2023-10-28 22:00:00 UTC" "2023-10-28 23:00:00 UTC"
#> [3] "2023-10-29 00:00:00 UTC" "2023-10-29 01:00:00 UTC"
#> [5] "2023-10-29 02:00:00 UTC" "2023-10-29 03:00:00 UTC"
```

Possibly we need `date_time_parse_UTC()` as one more convenience parser to fill this gap. I think this has come up one other time in the past. 

---

We'd end up with:

| <empty>  | UTC offset YES | UTC offset NO 
| ------------- | ------------- | ------------- |
| **Full TZ name YES** | date_time_parse_complete | date_time_parse_abbrev* | 
| **Full TZ name NO** | date_time_parse_UTC | date_time_parse |

With:
- `date_time_parse_abbrev()` being the `UTC offset NO + Full TZ name YES` combo, which isn't exactly accurate, but _just_ the full tz name like `America/New_York` is not enough to disambiguate a time that sits in the "fall back" overlap, so we don't include that case and instead include the abbrev case, because an abbreviation combined with the supplied `zone` is enough to disambiguate
- `date_time_parse_RFC_3339()` being a special case of `date_time_parse_UTC()` that is restricted to just the common RFC format

But then it seems like we actually cover the whole spectrum of possible formats to parse!

This table would probably be pretty useful to include in the help docs of `?date_time_parse`

title: Consider time_of_day class
description:
- Considered to be a calendar type
- Variable precision from hour -> nanosecond
- `time_of_day(hour, minute = NULL, second = NULL, subsecond = NULL, ..., subsecond_precision = NULL)`
- `get_*()` and `set_*()` methods
- No `add_*()` methods because I think wrap around arithmetic would just be confusing
- Comparison methods `>`, `<`, and equality `==` (if we had these, this is more reason not to have arithmetic, because wrap around arithmetic would conflict with comparision ops. in this way it works opposite of the weekday type which has circular arithmetic but no comparison ops)
- Consider that names would go on the `hour` field
- Can convert from time points, calendars, POSIXct, and durations as long as they have hour precision (consider what happens when converting from a duration goes out of the "conventional range")
- Can support parsing with custom template that returns the C++ hh_mm_ss object. Similar impl to ymd parser. Has a precision argument.
- Formatting could assume the day is 1970-01-01, and then give full `format` power.
- No way to go back to calendar / tp through an `as_*()` method.
- But we would have `as_duration()`. Then you can do `tp + as_duration(tod)`
- `calendar_group/narrow/widen()` all make sense
- Conversion to duration + duration-floor + conversion back is nice for rounding by things like 200 seconds

title: Add an FAQ entry for "No but really, I want POSIXct subseconds"
description:
After https://github.com/r-lib/clock/blob/adc01b61670b18463cc3087f1e58acf59ddc3915/vignettes/faq.Rmd#L216

Using this as an example
https://github.com/r-dbi/bigrquery/issues/591#issuecomment-1838942088

```r
bq_datetime_parse <- function(x) {
  # `format` matches clock already.
  # Bigquery DATETIME is documented as microsecond precision.
  # https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-types#datetime_type
  x <- clock::year_month_day_parse(x, precision = "microsecond")
  
  # Manually retain microseconds for the POSIXct
  microseconds <- clock::get_microsecond(x)
  microseconds <- microseconds / 1000000
  
  # Convert to POSIXct at second precision since that is what clock asserts
  # the precision of a POSIXct is. Can use sys-time since we are going straight
  # to UTC.
  x <- clock::calendar_narrow(x, "second")
  x <- clock::as_sys_time(x)
  x <- as.POSIXct(x, tz = "UTC")
  
  # Manually add microseconds back on (lossy, floating point issues!)
  x <- x + microseconds
  
  x
}
```

title: Question: ISO 8601 representations with reduced accuracy
description:
ISO 8601 allows for "representations with reduced accuracy," meaning that you can omit certain components of the date and time if they are not relevant or available. Here are some examples:

    Date Only:
        YYYY-MM-DD (complete)
        YYYY-MM (reduced accuracy, no day)
        YYYY (reduced accuracy, no month or day)

    Time Only:
        HH:MM:SS (complete)
        HH:MM (reduced accuracy, no seconds)
        HH (reduced accuracy, no minutes or seconds)

    Combined Date and Time:
        YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS (complete)
        YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM (reduced accuracy, no seconds)
        YYYY-MM-DDTHH (reduced accuracy, no minutes or seconds)

Is this supported in clock? I mean, is there a way to generate ISO 8601 strings with missing components, and indicate how those missing components are represented, e.g. with an hyphen? Are clock functions' implementation, in one way or the other, always going through `strftime()` or `strptime()`? As far as I understand these functions always impute the missing values to 0. Is there any low-level parser that collects all date-time components into a list before missing elements are converted to default values?

Here are examples of ISO 8601 dates or date-times that illustrate what I would like to achieve:

title: Any possibility of being less strict with sequence methods?
description:
I'm aware you've made some very deliberate design decisions in regards to the calendar classes, and what can be done with them, but would you consider being a little more flexible in some of the methods you provide? The motivation for this is to avoid downstream packages providing multiple, similar methods to work around some of the strictness.

As a concrete example, consider `<iso_year_week_day>` objects of varying precision. Quite often you would want something akin to calendar_spanning_seq that corresponds to valid *timepoints*. At present, due to the strictness of the class, I could envisage multiple implementations popping up similar to:

``` r
library(clock)

days <- iso_year_week_day(2021:2022, c(1L, 52L), 1L)
wks  <- calendar_narrow(days, "week")
yrs <- calendar_narrow(days, "year")

my_calendar_spanning_seq.clock_iso_year_week_day <- function(x) {
    
    df <- function(x) {
        out <- as_naive_time(x)
        out <- seq(min(out), max(out), by = 1L)
        as_iso_year_week_day(out)
    }
    
    wf <- function(x) {
        out <- calendar_widen(x, "day")
        out <- as_naive_time(out)
        out <- seq(min(out), max(out), by = 7L)
        out <- as_iso_year_week_day(out)
        calendar_narrow(out, "week")
    }
    
    precision <- calendar_precision(x)
    
    switch(
        precision,
        "day" = df(x),
        "week" = wf(x),
        "year" = calendar_spanning_seq(x),
        stop("Unsupported precision")
    )
}
```

I'm aware that you're still working on how you think {clock} is best utilised by other packages and for end users the benefit of the current approach is to make them explicitly handle these situations. However I'm hoping there is scope to maintain the minimalist class constructors but slightly increase the flexibility of the methods (balanced with increased documentation as to what the methods are doing).

I hope all this makes sense and no problem if you want to keep things as is (I just wanted to ensure I had raised it as a discussion point).

title: Implement `date_time_info()` and `zoned_time_info()`
description:
``` r
library(clock)

# Add input type checking
zoned_time_info <- function(x) {
  zone <- clock:::zoned_time_zone_attribute(x)
  x <- as_sys_time(x)
  out <- sys_time_info(x, zone)
  out$begin <- as_zoned_time(out$begin, zone = zone)
  out$end <- as_zoned_time(out$end, zone = zone)
  out
}

date_time_info <- function(x) {
  x <- as_zoned_time(x)
  out <- zoned_time_info(x)
  out$begin <- as_date_time(out$begin)
  out$end <- as_date_time(out$end)
  out
}

x <- date_time_parse("1970-10-25 00:00:00", "America/New_York")
x <- x + c(3600, 7200)

date_time_info(x)
#>                 begin                 end offset   dst abbreviation
#> 1 1970-04-26 03:00:00 1970-10-25 01:00:00 -14400  TRUE          EDT
#> 2 1970-10-25 01:00:00 1971-04-25 03:00:00 -18000 FALSE          EST
zoned_time_info(as_zoned_time(x))
#>                                         begin
#> 1 1970-04-26T03:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]
#> 2 1970-10-25T01:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]
#>                                           end offset   dst abbreviation
#> 1 1970-10-25T01:00:00-05:00[America/New_York] -14400  TRUE          EDT
#> 2 1971-04-25T03:00:00-04:00[America/New_York] -18000 FALSE          EST
```

These won't actually conflict with or be ambiguous with `naive_time_info()` in any way because we already know the time zone to look the information up in, and we know it is a `unique` type because the times exist already.

Follow up to https://github.com/r-lib/clock/pull/170 that does add `zoned_time_info()` back in. I feel like these wrappers are actually fairly useful and unambiguous.

Should make sure the begin/end limits are working right (year 32767 and whatnot)

title: The max/min values of time-points at different precisions are complex to figure out
description:
``` r
devtools::load_all()
#> ℹ Loading clock

# Largest possible minute precision duration on my Mac
# (would be smaller on Windows where the minute duration type is built on `int` not `int64_t`)
x <- new_duration_from_fields(list(ticks=2147483647L, ticks_of_day=1439L), PRECISION_MINUTE, NULL)
x
#> <duration<minute>[1]>
#> [1] 3092376453119
as_sys_time(x)
#> <time_point<sys><minute>[1]>
#> [1] "20599-06-22T23:59"

# Largest possible second precision duration (still room to go since this is an int64_t)
x <- new_duration_from_fields(list(ticks=2147483647L, ticks_of_day=86399L), PRECISION_SECOND, NULL)
x
#> <duration<second>[1]>
#> [1] 185542587187199
as_sys_time(x)
#> <time_point<sys><second>[1]>
#> [1] "20599-06-22T23:59:59"

# Largest possible millisecond precision duration (still room to go since this is an int64_t)
x <- new_duration_from_fields(list(ticks=2147483647L, ticks_of_day=86399L, ticks_of_second=999L), PRECISION_MILLISECOND, NULL)
x
#> <duration<millisecond>[1]>
#> [1] 185542587187199999
as_sys_time(x)
#> <time_point<sys><millisecond>[1]>
#> [1] "20599-06-22T23:59:59.999"

# Past the max int64_t value so it wrapped
x <- new_duration_from_fields(list(ticks=2147483647L, ticks_of_day=86399L, ticks_of_second=99999L), PRECISION_MICROSECOND, NULL)
x
#> <duration<microsecond>[1]>
#> [1] 1075146450103583839
as_sys_time(x)
#> <time_point<sys><microsecond>[1]>
#> [1] "-29496-01-13T15:41:43.583839"

# Real max microsecond value approaches max integer64 value (this is close to 9223372036854775807,
# but never actually reaches it because ticks_of_second wont get above 99999L)
x <- new_duration_from_fields(list(ticks=106751991L, ticks_of_day=14454L, ticks_of_second=99999L), PRECISION_MICROSECOND, NULL)
x
#> <duration<microsecond>[1]>
#> [1] 9223372036854099999
as_sys_time(x)
#> <time_point<sys><microsecond>[1]>
#> [1] "32103-01-10T04:00:54.099999"
```

This is a result of the way these are built with a breakdown of ticks/ticks-of-day/ticks-of-second. If all duration and time-point types used two doubles and stored a broken down int64_t value in there, then we could utilize the full range (which I think could be much larger!). This would be wasteful in terms of memory in many scenarios because often we only use `ticks`, like with day precision durations. This is only 4 bytes of memory (1 int) vs the 16 that would be required for 2 doubles. It would definitely simplify the codebase though, as the number of fields wouldn't vary anymore. We'd also have to consider how this works with proxies and comparisons (although I think I figured that out with integer64 in vctrs)

It gets even more complex because each platform decides what type can be used for each duration type:
General guidelines are here https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/duration
Windows implementation is here https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/standard-library/chrono?view=msvc-170#typedefs (notice `long long` for second but `int` for minute)
GCC implementation is here https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/16e2427f50c208dfe07d07f18009969502c25dc8/libstdc%2B%2B-v3/include/std/chrono#L816-L845 (notice int64_t for everything!)
Mac seems to use int64_t through hour, then switches to int for day

title: Consider removing `add_quarter()` method for Date and POSIXct
description:
Because "adding 1 quarter" is ambiguous. It could mean adding 3 months, or it could mean converting to year-quarter-day and adding 1 quarter, fixing the day of the quarter in place, then converting back to Date. These aren't always the same:

``` r
library(clock)

x <- as.Date(year_quarter_day(2019, 3, 92))
x
#> [1] "2019-09-30"

# These are the same (just because I defined it that way!)
add_quarters(x, 1)
#> [1] "2019-12-30"
add_months(x, 3)
#> [1] "2019-12-30"

# But that doesn't always align with this
as_year_quarter_day(x)
#> <year_quarter_day<January><day>[1]>
#> [1] "2019-Q3-92"
add_quarters(as_year_quarter_day(x), 1)
#> <year_quarter_day<January><day>[1]>
#> [1] "2019-Q4-92"
as.Date(add_quarters(as_year_quarter_day(x), 1))
#> [1] "2019-12-31"

# So it would be better to just have two options that are explicit:
add_months(x, 3)
#> [1] "2019-12-30"
as.Date(add_quarters(as_year_quarter_day(x), 1))
#> [1] "2019-12-31"
```

`add_weeks()` doesn't have this problem! It is always identical to `add_days(, n = 7)`.

We should review if there are any other places we allow `"quarter"` in the Date/POSIXt or possibly year-month-day API.

title: `date_difference()`, `calendar_difference()`, `time_point_difference()`
description:
```r
date_difference(x, ...)
date_difference.Date(x, ..., precision = y/q/m/w/d)
date_difference.POSIXt(x, ..., precision = y/q/m/w/d/H/M/S)

calendar_difference(x, ...)
calendar_difference.year_month_day(x, ..., precision = y/q/m)

time_point_difference(x, ...)
time_point_difference.year_month_day(x, ..., precision = w/d/H/M/S/subsecond
```

General idea is that these result in a data frame containing columns like `year`, `month`, ... down through the most precise component. If you were to add the components back to `from` in order of largest to smallest (does order matter?) bypassing intermediate invalid dates and time zone issues (by working with calendars and time points) then you'd end up with `to`

This would make it easy to compute someone's "age" in years as that is just `date_difference(a, b)$year` https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3611314/calculate-ages-in-r/25450756#25450756

Possibly first pass way to compute the months:
```
(date1.Year - date2.Year) * 12 + date1.Month - date2.Month + (date1.Day >= date2.Day ? 0 : -1)
```

Need to be very careful about the precisions that are allowed for calendar vs time point. I think ideally they don't overlap? i.e. day goes with time point.

The `precision` is used for the "starting" precision. i.e. `precision = "month"` would result in a data frame where the first column is the total number of whole months between the dates (although, this might be unnecessary cause you can always compute that from the year*12?)

Possibly the calendar and time point versions return data frames of duration columns, while the date version returns data frames of integer columns

_Possibly_ allow `from > to`, resulting in negative components. But this may be hard to define. It may "fall out" if we can define the algebraic property of the result. i.e. `from + (components) = to`

Non-year-month-day calendars would be useful too. like determining the number of iso weeks between dates

description:
Something like this, but done on the C++ side to be more efficient

``` r
library(clock)

formats_date <- c(
  # year, month, day
  "%Y-%m-%d",
  "%Y/%m/%d",
  "%Y.%m.%d",
  "%Y%m%d",
  
  "%Y %b %d",
  
  # month, day, year
  "%m-%d-%Y",
  "%m/%d/%Y",
  "%m.%d.%Y",
  "%m%d%Y",
  
  "%b %d %Y",
  "%b %d, %Y",
  "%b %dst %Y",
  "%b %dst, %Y",
  "%b %dnd %Y",
  "%b %dnd, %Y",
  "%b %drd %Y",
  "%b %drd, %Y",
  "%b %dth %Y",
  "%b %dth, %Y",
  
  # day, month, year
  "%d-%m-%Y",
  "%d/%m/%Y",
  "%d.%m.%Y",
  "%d%m%Y"
)

date_discover <- function(x) {
  worked <- vapply(
    formats_date, 
    function(format) {
      suppressWarnings({
        x <- date_parse(x, format = format)
      })
      any(!is.na(x))
    },
    logical(1)
  )
  
  formats_date[worked]
}

date_discover("2019-01-01")
#> [1] "%Y-%m-%d"

date_discover("April 1, 2020")
#> [1] "%b %d, %Y"
```

<sup>Created on 2021-10-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Would it take just 1 string as `x`? Or take a vector as `x` and report if there were any successes for a particular format?

Think about `January 1st, 2020` vs `January 2nd, 2020` and how to handle those suffixes. In that case it may be useful to allow a vector as `x` and it could report formats for `st`, `nd`, `rd`, `th`, etc

title: Parser for RFC 3339
description:
This is basically an even saner ISO 8601
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3339#page-4

It is stricter, and basically just offers 4 formats (plus optional fractional seconds)

```
%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ
%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%SZ # replace T with space

%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S+00:00 # replace Z with offset from UTC
%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S+00:00 # replace T with space
```

So we can do:

```r
library(clock)
library(rlang)

sys_time_parse_rfc3339 <- function(x, 
                                   ...,
                                   separator = "T",
                                   offset = "Z",
                                   precision = "second") {
  separator <- arg_match0(separator, values = c("T", "t", " "), arg_nm = "separator")
  offset <- arg_match0(offset, values = c("Z", "z", "%z"), arg_nm = "offset")
  format <- paste0("%Y-%m-%d", separator, "%H:%M:%S", offset)
  sys_time_parse(x, ..., format = format, precision = precision)
}

date_time_parse_rfc3339 <- function(x,
                                    ...,
                                    separator = "T",
                                    offset = "Z") {
  x <- sys_time_parse_rfc3339(x, ..., separator = separator, offset = offset, precision = "second")
  as.POSIXct(x, tz = "UTC")
}

foo <- c("2019-09-07T15:14:24Z", "2014-06-02T08:52:46Z", "2014-06-16T08:36:43Z")

date_time_parse_rfc3339(foo)
#> [1] "2019-09-07 15:14:24 UTC" "2014-06-02 08:52:46 UTC"
#> [3] "2014-06-16 08:36:43 UTC"

foo <- c("2019-09-07T15:14:24+01:00", "2014-06-02T08:52:46+01:00", "2014-06-16T08:36:43+01:30")

date_time_parse_rfc3339(foo, offset = "%z")
#> [1] "2019-09-07 14:14:24 UTC" "2014-06-02 07:52:46 UTC"
#> [3] "2014-06-16 07:36:43 UTC"
```

It nicely doesn't allow for local time in any way, so we can safely return UTC time stamps.

From my understanding in reading the RFC, the only optional part is fractional seconds, so we don't need to try and support a ton of formats that we have to guess through, which I really like

title: Should undefined date parsing error?
description:
I've been using date_parse to parse character inputs, from a user, in to dates with something akin to 
```
as_myclass.character <- function(x, format = NULL, locale = clock_locale(), ...) {
  check_dots_empty()
  x <- date_parse(x, format = format, locale = locale)
  if (all(is.na(x))) abort("Unable to parse any entries of x as Dates")
  vec_cast(x, new_myclass())
}
```
However I have just noticed the warning in the "Details" of the documentation:

> Parsing strings with sub-daily components, such as hours, minutes, or seconds, should be done with date_time_parse(). If you only need the date components, round the result to day precision, and then use as_date(). Attempting to directly parse a sub-daily string into a Date is ambiguous and undefined, and is unlikely to work as you might expect.

I had wrongly been assuming this would work similar to strptime where trailing characters were ignored
> strptime converts character vectors to class "POSIXlt": its input x is first converted by as.character. Each input string is processed as far as necessary for the format specified: any trailing characters are ignored.

This leads to the following question.  If passing a sub-standard daily string into a Date is undefined in clock would it be better for the following to error? 
```
clock::date_parse(c("2019-01-01 11", "2019-01-01 12"), format = "%Y-%m-%d")
```
Hope this makes sense.  This potentially links to #255

title: Move `master` branch to `main`

title: Does not compile on RHEL7/Centos - Parse errors with g++ 4.8.5 - possible solution provided
description:
### Issue Summary
Clock will not compile on RHEL7/Centos7 because 4.8.5 is the only supported c++ compiler version on those platforms.  

I have attached the output of the install.packages command to the end this ticket for the specific errors with date.h and error message 

> error: converting to ‘date::weekday’ from initializer list would use explicit constructor ‘constexpr date::weekday::weekday(unsigned int)’.

### Possible Solution
Howard Hinnant has provided a fix for this issue with a pre-compiler directive so that projects using his date library will compile under g++ 4.8.5.    

### Why Fix This?
RStudio Server is still supported for RHEL7/Centos7.  A lot of government enterprise RStudio Server installations still use RHEL7.

### Request
Could you please consider adding the the pre-compiler directive from HH below to make the clock package backwardly compatible with RHEL7/Centos7 systems running g++ 4.8.5?

### Reference
See: [Date Issue#264](https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date/issues/264)

> "Sorry, I forgot to mention that ONLY_C_LOCALE is required for pre-gcc-5.0.  
gcc-4.x doesn't have the C++11 std::time_get facets.  Setting ONLY_C_LOCALE to 1 tells the library to roll its own parsing/formatting without using the C++11 time facets, but it can only do so assuming the "C" locale."

title: Consider if `date_seq()`'s `to` argument really needs to match components to `from`
description:
Are there any cases where this becomes hard to define if we decide to be a bit more flexible?
Follow up to #218 

There are 3 combinations of optional arguments:

- `by` and `total_size`: This one isn't relevant for this discussion, since `to` isn't used
- `to` and `total_size`: This will always be generating a sequence at the precision of the input (day or second), so there are no components of `to` more precise than the precision of `by`, since `by` matches the precision of `to`
- `to` and `by`: This is where the changes would make an impact. See below.

I think that we cannot relax the assumption on `to` because of issues it could cause with >= daily precision `by`. For example:

```r
# DST gap from 01:59:59 -> 03:00:00 on the 26th
from <- date_time_build(1970, 04, 25, 02, 30, 00, zone = "America/New_York")
to <- date_time_build(1970, 04, 26, 03, 00, 00, zone = "America/New_York")

date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "shift-forward")
#> "1970-04-25 02:30:00 EST" "1970-04-26 03:30:00 EDT"

seq(from, to, by = "DSTday")
#> [1] "1970-04-25 02:30:00 EST" NA
```

In this example, the second element of the result would be past `to`, which isn't allowed.

```r
# Samoa skipped from 2011-12-29 23:59:59 -> 2011-12-31 00:00:00
from <- date_time_build(2011, 12, 29, 23, 30, 00, zone = "Pacific/Apia")
to <- date_time_build(2011, 12, 31, 02, 30, 00, zone = "Pacific/Apia")

date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "shift-forward")
#> "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"

seq(from, to, by = "DSTday")
#> [1] "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" NA
```

Similar problem as above

These issues could also be recreated with less precise precisions like year or month. Here is another case that shows that it is not restricted to DST gaps and weird DST changes. Here is an invalid date one:

```r
from <- date_build(1970, 01, 31)
to <- date_build(1970, 03, 01)

date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_months(1), invalid = "overflow")
#> "1970-01-31" "1970-03-03"

# WAT? I assume it tried to make `c(1970-01-31, 1970-03-03)` then filtered out the second
seq(from, to, by = "month")
#> [1] "1970-01-31"
```

It is impossible to have this issue if the time components of `from` and `to` match. In the worst case, you can have duplicate times, but this ensures that `date_seq()` always generates, at a minimum, a weakly increasing (or decreasing depending on the direction) sequence of dates.

``` r
library(clock)

from <- date_time_build(2011, 12, 29, 23, 30, 00, zone = "Pacific/Apia")
to <- date_time_build(2011, 12, 31, 23, 30, 00, zone = "Pacific/Apia")

date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "shift-forward")
#> [1] "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"
#> [3] "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"
date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "shift-backward")
#> [1] "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10"
#> [3] "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"

date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "roll-forward")
#> [1] "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" "2011-12-31 00:00:00 +14"
#> [3] "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"
date_seq(from, to = to, by = duration_days(1), nonexistent = "roll-backward")
#> [1] "2011-12-29 23:30:00 -10" "2011-12-29 23:59:59 -10"
#> [3] "2011-12-31 23:30:00 +14"
```

title: Discussion: The implied time zone of Date
description:
Currently, clock assumes that Date is UTC, because it seemed like this is also what base R assumed. I have now learned it is not quite that simple, and base R is actually inconsistent, treating Date as UTC or naive depending on the conversion being done

- Date -> POSIXct/lt, Date is treated as UTC (i.e. sys-time)
- POSIXct/lt -> Date, Date is treated as naive-time
- `Sys.Date()`, Date is treated as naive-time
- lubridate makes all of the same assumptions as base R, just with more intuitive defaults on a case-by-case basis. I still think it could be improved.

References:
- `?as.POSIXct.Date` states "Dates without times are treated as being at midnight UTC"
- `?as.Date.POSIXct` "(POSIXct and POSIXlt are) converted to days by ignoring the time after midnight in the representation of the time in specified time zone, default UTC"
- `?Sys.Date` states "Sys.Date returns the current day in the current time zone."
- Old comments from Ripley https://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/Date-conversion-with-as-POSIXct-and-as-POSIXlt-PR-9196-td912539.html

This begs the question, what is most useful for clock? A few places this comes up:

- `as.Date.clock_zoned_time` and `as_zoned_time.Date`
- Potential `date_today(zone = )` (Computed the current zoned-time, then convert to a Date, must assume naive or UTC) (#197)
- Potential `date_cast(x)` and `date_time_cast(x, zone, ..., nonexistent = , ambiguous =)` to be more consistent replacements for `as.Date()` and `as.POSIXct()`

It seems like it may be more intuitive if Date was treated as naive-time at all times.

``` r
# Date -> POSIXct
# - Date is treated as UTC
# - Resulting POSIXct uses the local time zone
# - No `tz` argument

x <- as.Date("2019-01-01")
x
#> [1] "2019-01-01"

# Date was treated as UTC, result shown in local time
as.POSIXct(x)
#> [1] "2018-12-31 19:00:00 EST"
clock::date_set_zone(as.POSIXct(x), "UTC")
#> [1] "2019-01-01 UTC"

as.POSIXct.Date
#> function (x, ...) 
#> .POSIXct(unclass(x) * 86400)
#> <bytecode: 0x7f8d54999538>
#> <environment: namespace:base>

# Date was treated as UTC, defaults to showing UTC time
# (same assumptions as R, just smarter defaults)
lubridate::as_datetime(x)
#> [1] "2019-01-01 UTC"
lubridate::as_datetime(x, tz = "America/New_York")
#> [1] "2018-12-31 19:00:00 EST"

# I'd argue that the above is probably still confusing,
# the user probably wanted to assume `x` was a naive-time
lubridate::force_tz(x, "America/New_York")
#> [1] "2019-01-01 EST"
```

``` r
# Date -> POSIXlt
# - Date is treated as UTC
# - Resulting POSIXlt uses UTC
# - No `tz` argument

x <- as.Date("2019-01-01")
x
#> [1] "2019-01-01"

as.POSIXlt(x)
#> [1] "2019-01-01 UTC"

as.POSIXlt.Date
#> function (x, ...) 
#> .Internal(Date2POSIXlt(x))
```

``` r
# POSIXct -> Date
# - Date is treated as naive
# - The current printed time of the POSIXct is converted to match `tz` without
#   changing the underlying duration (defaulting `tz` to UTC)
# - The new printed time is converted to a Date using `as.Date.POSIXlt`
# - `tz = "UTC"` by default

x <- as.POSIXct("2019-01-01 23:00:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles")
x
#> [1] "2019-01-01 23:00:00 PST"

# - `tz = "UTC"` by default
# - Printed time converted from America/Los_Angeles->UTC, then that is converted
#   to a Date, making the assumption that Date is a naive time

#> [1] "2019-01-02"

# - Just drop the time part and return a Date
# - Let Date be a naive type

as.Date.POSIXct
```

title: Non-Gregorian calendars?
description:
R currently has almost no support for dates in systems other than the standard Gregorian calendar, for example the Islamic, Persian, and other [regional and historic calendars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_calendars), [Gregorian variants](http://cfconventions.org/Data/cf-conventions/cf-conventions-1.7/cf-conventions.html#calendar), and astronomical [Julian dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_day). [chron](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=chron) and [oce](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=oce) have functions for converting Julian day numbers from/to POSIXt, [era](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=era) has classes for other calendars but only handles fractional years not dates, and `ConvCalendar` did a range of conversions but was removed from CRAN several years ago. To my knowledge that's about it. Representations of other calendars has been said to be out of the scope of lubridate in tidyverse/lubridate/issues/151 and tidyverse/lubridate/issues/756.

Would non-Gregorian calendars be in the scope of this package? I noticed that the underlying date library includes functionality for Julian and Tabular Islamic dates, and it seems the *calendar* system could be extended to many non-Gregorian systems?

title: Exposing low level sys/naive information
description:
- `sys_info`: Data frame with columns of sys-time begin, sys-time end, seconds offset, bool dst, string abbrev
- `sys_info(sys-time, zone)`
- `zoned_info()` would just hook into this and change the begin/end cols to zoned?

---

- `naive_info`: Data frame with columns of type (unique, nonexistent, ambiguous), first (a df-col of sys-info), second (a df-col of sys-info)
- `naive_info(naive-time, zone)`

---

To do something like `find_by_abbrev()`, take a single date-time string, parse to naive time, lookup naive info for each zone in `zone_database_names()`, look for unique types in which case we check the info abbrev against the one in the string for consistency, look for ambiguous types in which case the string abbrev breaks ambiguity, look for nonexistent types in which case we continue on

---

Oooh this is where we could take a vectorized `zone` argument for once. `sys_info(sys-time, zone)` where those two are recycled against each other. All columns of sys-info are zone independent, but contain the offset which is great for going from sys-time -> zoned-time for each zone.

And `naive_info(naive-time, zone)` with a vectorized zone would be useful for passing in the `zone_database_names()` all at once.

`naive_info(naive-time, zone)` with a vectorized zone also would be great for going from two independent columns of naive-time and zone to a single column of UTC time points

title: zoned_parse_abbrev()
description:
If a user has the following two strings:

```r
> before + 1
[1] "2020-11-01 01:00:00 EDT"
> before + 1 + 3600
[1] "2020-11-01 01:00:00 EST"
```

and prior knowledge that this is the America/New_York time zone, then:

- The user could supply a `zone = "America/New_York"` argument
- These strings could be parsed as naive-time, requiring that %Z be used, but ignoring %z
- Then converted to zoned-time with `zone`
- Then we could check that the parsed abbreviation matches the one in the sys-info (in the first slot of local-info) we get from converting from local->zoned
- If they don't match, then return NA with a warning
- If the local-info tells us this is a nonexistent time, return NA with a warning
- If the local-info tells us this is an ambiguous time, try to use the abbreviation in the string to resolve the ambiguity (as could be done above)

The zone abbreviation could be specified with `%Z`. 

This makes sense as a separate parser, since zoned-parse won’t ever have a zone argument.

we’d have a `date_time_parse_abbrev()` high level wrapper too

This is the same as:
https://github.com/HowardHinnant/date/wiki/Examples-and-Recipes#parse_daylight_transition

title: calendar_floor()/ceiling()/round()
description:
The idea here would be that the user could provide a calendar type that is less precise than the precision where invalid dates could happen for that calendar (so month or year for year-month-day, only year for iso-year-week-day). It would convert the calendar components to a duration (12*year+month=months), perform the rounding on that using duration-round, then convert back. An origin could be supplied as long as it is the same calendar and precision as the input.

This would allow you to floor sets of 20 months together

A key point is that this doesn’t round day precision calendar types up to month precision, as that crosses the calendrical/chronological barrier and isn’t well defined. Because of this, I don’t think it would be useful to have a date wrapper for this function. It would end up being more confusing than anything else.

Instead, we might consider limiting "common duration" ops to not be able to cross the week precision border (really day precision, but this is just 7 days).

This would let me remove the hacks added in the fix to #120, and would let me remove the "WARNING" labels in the documentation about duration arithmetic. I think it paints an overall clearer picture as well.

```
year / quarter / month

week / day / hour / minute / second / millisecond / microsecond / nanosecond
```

``` r
#> [1] year  month
```

title: Comparing between year-month-weekdays?
description:
The date library disables comparisons of `<` and `>` between them. The main reasoning is that you can't order weekdays, i.e. is Sunday before Saturday? Depends on where you start the week from. This also means you can't sort them.

Possibly disable `vec_proxy_compare()` (controlling `<`, `>`, min, max, median, quantile)? We would probably still want to enable `vec_proxy_order()`, since `group_by()` uses an ordering internally to get the groupings.

---

Alternatively we could assert that they will be ordered by day-of-month, like year-month-day, and override `vec_proxy_compare()` and `vec_proxy_order()` to cast to year-month-day and then return the proxy of that.

This would be somewhat consistent with the idea where casting year-month up to year-month-weekday defaults to the first day-of-month (no matter what weekday that is). And that flooring year-month-weekday to day will floor to the first day-of-month.

title: Duration model
description:
rcrd of 3 integer vectors hours/seconds/nanos - all with the same sign

Considering that date can support +/- ~33000 years, we should be able to support the full range with these 3 vectors since `33000*2*(365*24) = 578,160,000 hours` and that fits in an int. Then seconds has a range of [-3600,3600] and nanos has a range of [-999999999, 999999999]. 

Always displays to the user as `seconds.nanos`, using an int64_t to hold the seconds computed from hours * 3600 + seconds, which should always fit in an int64_t.

From there we could do arithmetic using `add_hours(<duration>, 1)`. We could even have `add_years(<duration>, 1)` which would use the C++20 definition of a year duration.

This type would be the result of `naive_nano_datetime - naive_nano_datetime`

It would then be possible to define `add_duration(x, duration)`

title: Should only arithmetic drop time of day by default?
description:
i.e. does `end-keep` and `next-shift` unambiguously make more sense here without potential for loss of relative ordering?

```r
> adjust_year(as.POSIXct("1972-02-29"), 1973)
[1] "1973-02-28 23:59:59 EST"
> adjust_year(as.POSIXct("1972-02-29"), 1973, day_nonexistent = "end-keep")
[1] "1973-02-28 EST"

> adjust_day(as.POSIXct("1970-04-20 02:30:30", "America/New_York"), 26)
[1] "1970-04-26 03:00:00 EDT"
> adjust_day(as.POSIXct("1970-04-20 02:30:30", "America/New_York"), 26, dst_nonexistent = "next-shift")
[1] "1970-04-26 03:30:30 EDT"
```

this would explain why java time uses end-keep as the default

also consider `dst_ambiguous = "offset"` as a way to resolve ambiguous times by choosing the same offset as the original time where possible.

title: Wrap `adjust_last_*()` functions into their non-last equivalents
description:
`adjust_last_day_of_month()` -> `adjust_day(x, "last")`
`adjust_last_day_of_quarter()` -> `adjust_quarterday(x, "last")`
`adjust_last_weeknum_of_year()` -> `adjust_weeknum(x, "last")`

Pass on `"last"` to the C++ code by overwriting `value` with `-1L` to signal that we don't need it, and by setting a boolean argument of `last` to `true`. This way, a user won't be able to accidentally use `last = c(-1L, 1L)` and have that work because it matches our internal representation of last (the `check_*()` functions would catch that).

title: Fiscal calendar tweaks
description:
Consider:

```

quarter -> quarternum
day -> quarterday
```

This would more closely match `year_weeknum_weekday()`, and would have less confusion about what `"day"` means since it would explicitly be `"quarterday"`. This would mean we would get `adjust_quarterday()` rather than `adjust_day()`, and `adjust_quarternum()` rather than `adjust_quarter()`, but I think that is also less confusing

title: Rework local datetime on top of vctrs rcrd
description:
It should be a field based type, i.e. like

```r
list(year = , month = , day = , hour = , minute = , second =)
```

Building off this type allows complete control over the `!ok()` case, which allows you to do things like

```r
as.Date("2019-01-31") %>%
  localize() %>%
  add_months(1) %>% # prints 2019-02-31 which is a !ok() datetime, but thats fine right now
  adjust_day(5) %>% # prints 2019-02-05 which is now ok()
  unlocalize()
```

Resolve `!ok()` ness with `resolve()` or something similar

```r
as.Date("2019-01-31") %>%
  localize() %>%
  add_months(1) %>% # prints 2019-02-31
  resolve(day_nonexistent = "last-day") # prints 2019-02-28
```

^ Maybe a set of resolvers like `resolve_last_day()` or `resolve_last_time()`

For arithmetic, if adding day/hour/minute/second and `!ok()` then this isn't defined. In those cases we throw a warning and suggest that the user resolve with `resolve()` and then auto resolve with `day_nonexistent = "last-time"`

`unlocalize()` would gain a `day_nonexistent` arg to handle nonexistent cases that havent already been handled
